PART I
ITEM 1. BUSINESS

Acme Widgets, Inc. designs, manufactures and sells industrial widgets and the software that schedules them. We serve customers in the automotive, aerospace and consumer segments through direct sales and a network of distributors. Our products are sold under the Acme and WidgetPro brands.

We compete on precision, delivery time and total cost of ownership. Our manufacturing runs in two plants in Ohio and one in Monterrey, Mexico. We hold 112 issued patents and rely on trade secrets for our alloy formulations. As of December 31 we employed approximately 2,400 people, none of whom are represented by a union.

Our fiscal year ends on December 31. Seasonality is modest; the fourth quarter is typically the strongest because automotive customers take delivery ahead of model-year changes. Raw material costs, chiefly specialty steel and copper, are the largest component of cost of goods sold.

Item 1A.  Risk Factors

Investing in our common stock involves risk. You should consider carefully the risks described below, as well as the other information in this report, including Item 7 of this report, before making an investment decision.

Our business depends on a small number of large customers. Our ten largest customers accounted for 58% of revenue. The loss of any one of them, or a significant reduction in their orders, would materially reduce our revenue and profitability.

We are subject to a pending investigation by the Department of Commerce concerning the country of origin labelling of certain alloy components sourced through our Monterrey facility. We cannot predict the outcome, the timing, or the penalties, which could include fines, import restrictions and the suspension of our ability to sell to federal government contractors. Responding to the investigation has diverted management attention and will increase legal expense in the coming year.

Our largest automotive customer has notified us that it intends to dual-source widgets beginning next model year. If it shifts a substantial share of its volume to the second supplier, our revenue, plant utilisation and margins would decline. We have not yet secured replacement volume.

Covenants in our amended credit agreement now require a minimum fixed-charge coverage ratio that we may not meet if the automotive volume declines as described above; a covenant breach would permit our lenders to accelerate the debt and restrict our ability to pay dividends.

Increases in the price of specialty steel and copper, or disruptions in their supply, could raise our costs faster than we can pass them to customers under fixed-price contracts.

Recently enacted tariffs on goods crossing the Mexican border apply to substantially all output of our Monterrey plant, and the exemptions we previously relied upon have been withdrawn. We are evaluating relocation of some production, which would require significant capital expenditure and cause transition disruption.

A failure of our information systems, including a cybersecurity incident, could disrupt manufacturing scheduling and expose us to liability and reputational harm.

ITEM 2. PROPERTIES

Item 3. Legal Proceedings

From time to time we are involved in litigation arising in the ordinary course of business, including product liability and employment claims. We do not believe that any currently pending matter, individually or in the aggregate, will have a material adverse effect on our financial position, results of operations or cash flows. Refer to Note 14 of the consolidated financial statements for additional information regarding legal matters and the accrual we have recorded.

PART II
ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

Revenue increased 6% to $842 million, driven by higher automotive volumes and a 3% price increase implemented in the second quarter, partially offset by lower aerospace shipments. Gross margin was 31.2% compared with 30.4% in the prior year, reflecting the price increase and manufacturing efficiencies at our Ohio plants, offset in part by higher copper costs.

Selling, general and administrative expenses increased 4% due to headcount additions in sales and higher incentive compensation. Operating income was $118 million, or 14.0% of revenue. Interest expense declined as we repaid $40 million of term debt. Our effective tax rate was 23%.

Cash provided by operating activities was $131 million. Capital expenditures were $52 million, primarily for the Monterrey capacity expansion. We ended the year with $96 million in cash and $210 million available under our revolving credit facility. We believe our liquidity is sufficient to fund operations, capital expenditures and debt service for at least the next twelve months.

Critical accounting estimates include revenue recognition on long-term contracts, inventory valuation, goodwill impairment testing and warranty reserves, as described in Note 2.

ITEM 7A. QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK

We are exposed to commodity price risk on copper and to foreign currency risk on the Mexican peso. A 10% change in the peso would change annual operating income by approximately $4 million.
